content: By 2030, the global burden of deaths and disabilities caused by snakebite envenoming is expected to be significantly reduced through targeted interventions. Community education plays a critical role in mitigating the risk of snakebite envenoming by raising awareness about prevention and encouraging health-seeking behaviors. Snakebite envenoming disproportionately affects young, healthy, and productive members of communities, often those who are essential contributors to their families and local economies. These individuals may be responsible for food production, childcare, elder care, and other vital community functions. When they are bitten, the impact extends beyond their personal health to the well-being of their families and communities. A comprehensive strategy emphasizes the importance of engaging communities to promote education about snakebite risks, prevention, and the need for timely medical care. This approach integrates snakebite awareness into broader health and environmental programs, empowering communities to take proactive measures. Active community participation is essential for the success of these initiatives, as a bottom-up approach is more effective than external interventions. Collaboration with local leaders, civil society, and health activists enhances outcomes. In many regions, there is a lack of reliable data on the burden and impact of snakebite envenoming, making it difficult to measure the success of interventions. Systematic baseline data collection will provide insights into the burden of snakebite envenoming, its effects on communities, and the long-term impact of interventions. Operational research will evaluate prevention strategies, including snake avoidance and risk reduction, to validate affordable and context-appropriate interventions. Community consultation and research are critical for understanding local perceptions, socio-cultural factors, and spiritual beliefs about snakes and snakebites. This information will guide the design of prevention initiatives tailored to specific communities. Strategies that work in one setting may not be effective in others, highlighting the need for localized approaches. Research on human-animal interactions and ecological risk factors will inform prevention efforts and improve understanding of venomous snake ecology. First aid and pre-hospital care are fundamental to reducing mortality and improving outcomes. Training community first responders in safe and effective snakebite first aid is essential. Ambulance personnel must also be trained to manage life-threatening complications during transport, such as severe shock, hemorrhage, airway obstruction, or respiratory paralysis. Supervised and well-equipped ambulance services are a critical component of a functioning health system, ensuring timely access to appropriate care. Improving health-seeking behavior is vital, as many victims rely on traditional medicine or spiritual healers, often with poor outcomes. Understanding the factors influencing these decisions will help design interventions to encourage the use of allopathic medicine. Engaging traditional healers and influential community members to support better health-seeking behavior can lead to improved outcomes. Access to high-quality antivenoms is crucial for effective treatment. Antivenoms must meet international standards for safety and efficacy. However, many regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia, face shortages of effective antivenoms due to weak manufacturing and market instability. Strategic investment in antivenom production, regulation, and distribution is necessary to ensure availability and affordability. By 2030, the goal is to provide universal access to safe and effective antivenoms. Research into next-generation treatments and innovative medical interventions is essential to improve outcomes. Clinical trials and operational research will optimize treatment protocols and inform national health worker training programs. Strengthening health systems and infrastructure will further enhance the delivery of care. Global risk-benefit assessments of antivenom products will identify suitable treatments for each WHO region. Poor-quality products undermine market confidence and contribute to market fragility. WHO will provide guidance, standards, and technical support to regulatory agencies to ensure the safety, efficacy, and quality of antivenoms. Prequalification processes and reference standards for venoms and antivenoms will be established to improve product evaluation and market confidence. Cost-mitigation schemes will address financial barriers to treatment, reducing socioeconomic hardship and improving clinical outcomes. Local political commitment and financial investment are critical to the success of these interventions. Public-private partnerships will support antivenom production in lowand middle-income countries, contributing to a sustainable market and achieving a 25% increase in manufacturers by 2030. In summary, a multifaceted approach involving community engagement, education, research, improved access to antivenoms, and strengthened health systems is essential to reduce the global burden of snakebite envenoming.
